claims.text: Adding a minor fraction of vanadium to a refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its radiation tolerance.
Vanadium addition will promote irradiation-induced defect recombination.
Vanadium addition will establish stable nanoscale defect sinks.
The proposed vanadium addition will preserve mechanical integrity under plasma-facing conditions.
The baseline is a tungsten-tantalum-based refractory high-entropy alloy without vanadium alloying.
The intervention is addition of 2–5 atomic percent vanadium.
The hypothesized effect is expected under krypton-ion irradiation at approximately 350–600 °C.
Vanadium addition will produce uniform vanadium-rich clusters or nanoscale precipitates.
The vanadium-rich clusters or nanoscale precipitates will act as sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
Increasing defect-sink density will promote recombination of vacancies and interstitials.
Enhanced vacancy-interstitial recombination will reduce the overall irradiation-induced defect concentration.
The vanadium-induced microstructural changes will not significantly alter the alloy's primary mechanical properties.
The vanadium-alloyed material will have 20–30% lower irradiation-induced defect density than the unmodified baseline.
The vanadium-alloyed material will retain yield strength within ±10% of the unmodified baseline.
The effect should hold only while the vanadium content remains low enough to avoid destabilizing the alloy's phase structure.
Larger vanadium additions or operation outside 350–600 °C may cause phase changes or performance degradation.
The precise improvement and optimal vanadium content are uncertain and require experimental optimization.
Long-term mechanical performance under fusion-reactor conditions remains uncertain.
The experiment compares a 2–5 at.% vanadium-modified alloy against an unmodified control under otherwise identical krypton-ion irradiation at approximately 400 °C.
The hypothesis is falsified if the modified alloy fails to achieve the specified defect-density reduction or if its yield strength differs from the control by more than ±10%.
